In simulations, the monitor gained 0.13 in area under the precision-recall curve on larger oscillator networks with familiar topologies and 0.09 on larger networks with held-out topologies, relative to a graph baseline without propagation features. Gains were small in contractive consensus. Giving the graph baseline the same features narrowed the gap. In a separate planning study, ensemble simulation recovered about 99% of the possible improvement over random intervention selection in oscillators and nearly all of it in consensus. With a simplified oscillator twin, selecting by predicted outcome also gave lower regret than selecting by trajectory fidelity. These results show when propagation features help flag unreliable forecasts and why the quality of intervention choices should be measured directly.

2611.28507.title: A generative framework for unified representations bridging electrophysiological and haemodynamic brain activity
2611.28507.abstract: Electrophysiological and haemodynamic recordings resolve brain activity at complementary temporal and spatial scales, yet paired acquisition remains difficult to scale. We propose a generative framework that aligns paired multimodal recordings in a unified representation space and generates modality-specific haemodynamic responses from EEG. In paired cohorts, the framework generated fMRI BOLD and fNIRS haemoglobin responses that reproduced regional dynamics, cortical maps, functional connectivity and task structure. Generated BOLD followed Real BOLD time courses and cortical patterns, while Generated haemoglobin responses tracked task-evoked HbO and HbR dynamics. The framework enabled decoding across visual, motor-imagery and mental-arithmetic tasks, independent-record decoding, external BOLD localization and low-sample augmentation. Paired feature-space calibration supported bidirectional retrieval. The proposed framework extends cortical analysis and brain decoding to EEG recordings when Real haemodynamic data are sparse.

2611.28497.title: When AI Performance Is Not Enough: Statistical Guardrails for Clinical Development
2611.28497.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are reshaping the operational and inferential landscape of clinical development, yet their adoption frequently outpaces the statistical scrutiny these methods demand. This commentary offers first-principles perspectives across four application domains: anomaly detection in clinical trial data, real-time monitoring and adaptive trial designs, biomarker-based enrichment, and virtual and digital twins. For each domain, we articulate the underlying inferential problem, the contribution of AI and ML relative to established statistical methods, and the risks that statisticians, data scientists, and clinical developers must actively manage. Across these domains, a unifying theme emerges: AI and ML methods may succeed locally while failing to satisfy the broader statistical assumptions required for valid clinical and regulatory decisions. These risks include false-positive signals, compromised Type I error control in adaptive designs, conflation of prognostic with predictive biomarkers, and causal claims not supported by data and assumptions. We argue that a clearly defined context of use, relevant statistical assumptions, and consequences of the intended decision should guide the evaluation. For treatment-effect questions, the ICH E9(R1) estimand framework provides a useful organizing principle. Responsible use of AI in clinical development requires not restraint, but rigor: the inferential discipline necessary to make these technologies reproducible, interpretable, and defensible in the service of patients.

2611.28491.title: SoK: Splitting the Trigger or Adding Attackers? Disentangling Distributed Backdoor Attacks in Federated Learning
2611.28491.abstract: Distributed backdoor attacks split a trigger among several federated learning clients, so that the backdoor appears only in the aggregated model. Since DBA, a line of work has reported that such attacks are stronger, more persistent, and stealthier than a single attacker with the full trigger. We systematize this literature and test this belief. We code nineteen primary studies and fifteen papers that evaluate against DBA. The reported advantage is rarely measured against a complete trigger delivered by the same attackers, and none of the fifteen evaluations tests whether individual pieces remain effective. We then run 875 paired federated runs that separate adding attackers from splitting the trigger. In our image experiments, adding attackers raised attack success in every seed of all 30 cells where we measured it, by 7.5 to 83.4 percentage points on average. Splitting the trigger among the same attackers had a smaller effect, and its sign depended on the piece layout, the allocation, and the attackers' local training. With DBA's compact layout, splitting lowered attack success on CIFAR-10. A larger penalty on small CNNs vanished once the attackers trained longer, and an FCBA-style allocation gained a few points. Widely separated pieces helped on CIFAR-10, its grayscale version, and GTSRB. No model required all pieces. Neural Cleanse suppressed single pieces together with the full trigger, but split backdoors with separated pieces survived it better than complete ones. We derive reporting requirements for attack and defense evaluations.

2611.28483.title: Don't Train It, Write It: An AI Agent Writes New Capabilities into Language Model Weights
2611.28483.abstract: We show that an AI agent can write new capabilities into a pretrained language model by adding gated attention heads and MLP neurons inside its existing layers, without backpropagation and without fitting any weight to the answers of task examples. It has a budget of 50 model passes and sees no validation or test instance. Composed in one model, its modules for six BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) subtasks raise the normalized BBH score of Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct from 19.95 to 41.05 (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct: at most 35.01) and that of Gemma-3-1B-it from 10.25 to 32.86. Against the unmodified model at the same precision, both composites leave the next-token distribution on 1,023,000 WikiText tokens unchanged (KL exactly 0), give identical answers on 15,845 items of five other Leaderboard tests and identical scores on the other 18 BBH subtasks. The agent also writes exact multiplication up to 20 digits, running the model only up to 6 (100.0% on the absent lengths of the sealed test in both models; a LoRA with the same budget: at most 2.1%). Sets, rules and report sentences were sealed in git before the first session (manifests timestamped in Bitcoin), with dated amendments listed in Appendix D; a frozen evaluator ran the sealed test once. Verdicts (H5: tracking; H6: composite; H8: one pass vs. chain of thought; H9: fresh and rewritten instances; H10: side effects; H12: multiplication), on the preregistered sealed test, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct: H5 success, H6 success, H8 (web_of_lies) success, H9 success, H10 (composite) success on (i) to (iii), (iv) confirmed, H12 success; Gemma-3-1B-it (H7: H5, H6, H8 and H9 in this model): H5 success, H6 success, H8 (web_of_lies) success, H8 (tracking 3) success, H9 partial, H10 (composite) success on (i) to (iii), (iv) confirmed, H12 success. Not everything worked: 4 of 45 single modules show small side effects and 5 of 50 sessions hit the 12-hour limit without a module.

2611.28476.title: PAMS: Preconditioned Activation-Metric Subspace for Zeroth-Order LLM Fine-tuning
2611.28476.abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization provides a computationally efficient approach to fine-tuning large language models (LLMs), but conventional methods typically rely on isotropic perturbations that ignore the anisotropic structure of neural-network parameter spaces. We introduce Preconditioned Activation-Metric Subspace (PAMS), a ZO optimization framework that uses forward-pass activation statistics to construct structured, layer-wise perturbation geometries without computing gradients or forming dense curvature matrices. PAMS tracks a low-rank approximation of the dominant activation subspace and its associated spectrum online, and uses the spectrum to softly reweight perturbation variance while preserving exploration in directions outside the retained subspace. A trace normalization separates the perturbation geometry from its overall scale, enabling consistent perturbation magnitudes across layers. We show theoretically that the resulting perturbation covariance induces right-side preconditioning of the gradient of the corresponding Gaussian-smoothed objective. We further characterize the estimator's smoothing bias and second moment and derive a nonconvex convergence guarantee that captures the effects of the perturbation geometry and smoothing radius. The proposed low-rank tracking procedure requires $\mathcal{O}(n_l r)$ persistent memory for a layer with input dimension nl and retained rank r, avoiding the $\mathcal{O}(n_l^2)$ memory required by a dense activation covariance. Experiments on transformer-based language-model fine-tuning tasks across GLUE and SuperGLUE demonstrate that PAMS improves the effectiveness and stability of zeroth-order optimization while retaining its gradient-free and objective-evaluation-based advantages.

2611.28469.title: Automated Safety Analysis for Agentic Workflows
2611.28469.abstract: LLM applications are increasingly built as agentic workflows: programs that combine model calls, external tools, and control logic to act autonomously on a user's behalf. Because these workflows execute real-world actions, logical flaws in how a workflow is wired can cause severe harm in deployed systems. Unlike prompt injections or malformed API calls, these workflow bugs stem from defects in the workflow's design, yet no existing tool can statically validate workflow logic across frameworks prior to deployment. We present Apsis, a static safety analyzer that detects workflow bugs before deployment. To operate across frameworks, Apsis lifts framework-specific code into a common intermediate representation (IR). This IR models a workflow as a semantic graph of steps, data dependencies, and shared state, while annotating each component with behavioral properties such as whether an input is mandatory or how a shared channel merges concurrent writes. Building on this representation, we introduce a bug description language that formalizes recurring classes of agentic failures as declarative patterns over the IR. By matching these patterns against the IR, Apsis detects structural and behavioral flaws and pinpoints the exact step responsible for each bug. To evaluate Apsis, we construct, to our knowledge, the first corpus of workflow bugs, distilled from real-world reports across 13 widely used frameworks. On a reproducible benchmark suite drawn from this corpus, Apsis detects workflow bugs with 91% precision and 84% recall, and uncovers 36 previously unknown bugs in real-world workflows.

2611.28465.title: HiPPO Functional Memory: Coordinate-Queryable Attention for Irregular Time Series
2611.28465.abstract: Irregular time series are recorded at nonuniform times and are often queried at other times: between observations, after the last one, or on a regular grid. Continuous-time models answer such queries by integrating latent dynamics, and time-aware attention models answer them by revisiting the observation tokens. We introduce HiPPO Functional Memory (HiPPO-FM), an attention operator that writes an irregular history into a rank-M function space with explicit time coordinates. Masked self-attention first exchanges content among the observations; the updated values are then contracted against kernel-smoothed HiPPO-Legendre features and solved through a regularized Gram matrix, so the retained coefficients define a function that is read at any time through the same features. The write and read have the form of an interdomain sparse Gaussian-process mean: every readout lies in an M-dimensional reproducing-kernel subspace, and a pointwise bound separates the approximation error of this subspace from the error of the learned memory. Removing the functional memory from the encoder raises Spiral reconstruction RMSE 18-fold. The full model has the lowest error in 11 of 12 Spiral settings, the highest overall accuracy and best average rank on 20 irregular UEA datasets, the highest event-type accuracy on all five multi-type event benchmarks, and a 21% lower extrapolation MSE than CRU on PhysioNet. Because the memory has fixed rank, the state retained after encoding keeps a fixed size as the history grows and is 102 times smaller than a token cache at 1,024 observations.

2611.28451.title: Guidance-Induced Activation of Score Estimation Errors in Diffusion Models
2611.28451.abstract: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) combines conditional and unconditional score estimates to steer diffusion sampling. The weighted-solenoidal component of each score error has no instantaneous effect on the evolution of its corresponding reference density. Because the guided density in CFG generally differs from both reference densities, the combination of these solenoidal components can affect the evolution of the guided marginals. We call this mechanism guidance-induced error activation. Using a weighted Helmholtz-Hodge decomposition, we identify the activated error field, quantify its magnitude, and characterize when it vanishes. At fixed noise time, the activated error field varies continuously with guidance strength. Its weak first-order variation has two terms, one from reweighting the errors and one from the change in the guided density. For finite score errors, ODE characteristics and an SDE Feynman-Kac formula connect error-activation to the generated densities. For a class of finite Gaussian mixtures, error-activation can account for most of the KL divergence between the generated distributions by learned-score and exact-score CFG ODE samplers under strong guidance. Ideal score filtering removes the weighted-solenoidal errors and eliminates error-activation. Controlled experiments with Gaussian and Gamma mixtures illustrate how activation affects the generated densities. Qualitative CIFAR-10 comparisons suggest that filtering can help preserve object structure under strong guidance.

2611.28430.title: Lean Census: A Distributional Analysis of AI-Generated Lean Code
2611.28430.abstract: We compare two human-written and four AI-generated Lean libraries with Mathlib through the distributions of simple statistics of their code. For each library we measure inline claims in proofs, proof length, how often each declaration is used, and design choices such as instances and private declarations, and we read each against the variation among Mathlib's own areas. The AI-generated libraries have more inline claims per theorem, longer proofs, fewer instances, and more private declarations than the human-written ones. We release the code for the analysis as a package, lean-census, at https://github.com/project-numina/lean-census.

2611.28426.title: When AI Should Not Decide: Evidence Sufficiency and Decision Stability in Automated Job Interviews
2611.28426.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to assess employment candidates, yet consistent interview scoring does not establish whether automated recommendations are supported by sufficient evidence. This study introduces the Evidence Sufficiency and Decision Stability Assessment (ESDSA), which combines criterion-level evidence classification, deterministic quotation traceability and stability checks across linguistic variants assessed as substantively equivalent. We evaluated four approaches (scoring-only, evidence-aware, traceability-based and integrated ESDSA v2) using 540 synthetic interview responses from 60 evaluated scenario families across Software Engineering, Customer Support and Operations. In held-out testing (216 responses), integrated ESDSA achieved 85.19% actionable coverage and 3.80% disagreement among actionable recommendations against AI-assisted provisional references. Evidence-aware evaluation achieved 92.59% coverage and 4.50% disagreement; scoring-only evaluation achieved 71.30% coverage and 1.95% disagreement. The integrated stability gate deferred 11 additional previously actionable decisions, ten of which had agreed with provisional references. The findings demonstrate trade-offs between evidential constraints, decision consistency and abstention, rather than overall superiority of the integrated framework. ESDSA offers a reproducible methodology for examining when automated interview recommendations should be actionable or deferred. Synthetic responses and AI-assisted references do not establish real-world recruitment validity.

2611.28418.title: WingBench: Benchmarking How AI Agents Search for Better Designs
2611.28418.abstract: Design search often uses cheap learned predictions to choose which candidates deserve expensive tests, but these tests can fail, especially on the unusual designs that optimization favors. We introduce WingBench, a multifidelity benchmark in which optimizers and AI agents design transonic wings with computational fluid dynamics (CFD) inside the search. They can query a learned aerodynamic surrogate and spend a fixed budget of sequential CFD evaluations, each returning a score or a failure type. WingBench grades the design each method recommends, reporting separately whether it receives a valid score and how good that score is. Using WingBench, we contribute a study of five baseline optimizers and a comparison of three AI agent methods, which produced 6,629 CFD evaluation records. Feedback helps baseline optimizers deliver valid designs when it changes their later proposals, but the differential-evolution variant does so with lower aerodynamic quality. An open-ended research agent finds designs of similar quality to the strongest baselines over 32 CFD queries, with different prior information and unmatched total computation. In early search, our reflection and planning implementations do not consistently improve on it. We release the data, code, agent prompts, and analysis scripts for reproducibility.

2611.28405.title: When Can an AI Agent Serve as a Model of Human Psychopathology?
2611.28405.abstract: Language models and AI agents are increasingly described in psychiatric terms, such as anxious, depressed, addicted or helpless. A recent study even proposed language models as experimental systems for psychiatry and as a platform for piloting psychological treatments. We ask when an experiment on an AI agent can provide evidence about a specified human psychiatric process. A claim to such evidence has three parts. Something changed in the agent, and the agent's history caused the change. Nothing other than a process shared with people explains that change. The change matches one theory of the human process and not that theory's rivals. Psychiatry and its neighbouring fields have an evidence standard for each part, from the diagnostic manuals' rule for induced states, from clinical test scores and from animal models. We translate each standard into a criterion that a machine study can meet. For a language model the most critical alternative to a shared process is extrapolation from its training text, which already contains descriptions of how people respond to trauma and how they answer questionnaires. We show how to probe that alternative. Further, we audited forty-three published studies that apply psychiatric terms to a machine or induce a comparable state in one. Most compared the machine with an identical copy that had not gone through the history that induced the state. None excluded extrapolation from training text. Three tested a psychiatric theory against its rivals, and none of the three tests was conclusive. Until better evidence exists, a treatment pilot on a language model is best read as the model's forecast of patient response, and not as an experiment on a model organism. Evidence for a model organism will come from states induced by what happens to the machine, from experiments on its internal workings, and from tests on which rival theories disagree.

2611.28396.title: Targeted In-Context Poisoning of Tabular Foundation Models: An Empirical Study
2611.28396.abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) predict the label of a query row conditioned on a context of labelled rows, without training on them. Drawn from operational data, the context becomes an attack surface. We study targeted in-context poisoning in its simplest form: an attacker with write access to the context's source places exact copies of a target row there with the wrong label. On 30 OpenML datasets for binary classification, one such poison row flips on average 53% (TabICL) and 65% (TabPFN) of the predictions correct without attack, and three poison rows flip almost all. The same copy with the true label flips almost none, and performance on the remaining rows hardly changes. Predictions flip by two routes: in TabICL, the target row's embedding rotates towards the mean of the wrong class; in TabPFN, the poison row pulls genuine rows of the wrong class along. The TFMs thus infer soundly, but from forged evidence. Predictions of trained models flip as well: almost always for a random forest, for CatBoost as often as for the TFMs, hardly for a logistic regression. New with TFMs is not the kind of vulnerability but the timing: the data take effect at the moment of prediction, not through training, and a poison row in a live context can be deleted afterwards. Three established requirements must therefore cover the context: access control for its source, traceability per prediction, which can also deter, and validation at prediction time. A detection mechanism shows how such validation can work.

2611.28374.title: Taking the PULSE of Enterprise Workflows: Evaluating Persistent Project-State Understanding
2611.28374.abstract: Enterprise agents must maintain an up-to-date understanding of work distributed across heterogeneous artifacts, evolving over time, and unevenly visible to different collaborators. We formulate this challenge as persistent project-state understanding (PPSU) and introduce PULSE, a benchmark of 1,573 questions over 30 enterprise project histories. PULSE constructs deterministic, time-indexed project state and documented collaborator views from source-linked records, and evaluates three families of questions: open loops, project evolution, and view gaps. Across retrieval agents, graph- and memory-augmented retrieval, long-context, and oracle conditions, we find substantial headroom for current systems. Retrieval and extraction account for the largest share of the gap, but providing explicit project state on top of gold evidence yields further substantial gains, showing that PPSU cannot be reduced to retrieval alone. Further analysis shows that questions requiring information to be reconciled across multiple parts of the project history remain difficult even when the relevant evidence is provided, while project-state synthesis and perspective conditioning remain persistent challenges. These results motivate enterprise agents that explicitly maintain and reconcile temporally grounded state across sources, actors, and time.

2611.28366.title: Cross-Site Transformers Are Robust Heart Rate Estimators
2611.28366.abstract: Single-site heart-rate estimation from photoplethysmography (PPG) degrades sharply under real-world motion. Multi-site PPG provides a natural solution, but existing models fuse sites as generic sensor channels rather than exploiting their hemodynamic structure: each heartbeat propagates along the arterial tree, appearing across body sites as delayed and transformed copies of the same cardiac event. We propose the Cross-Site Transformer, which introduces a hemodynamically informed inductive bias by restricting multi-sensor fusion to cross-attention between PPG sites. On WildPPG, the largest in-the-wild benchmark available, our model establishes a new single-model state of the art, reducing error by 21% over the previous best and 35% over the best prior transformer. The same cross-site restriction makes the trained network directly auditable. Because each cross-attention head lies on one directed pathway between sites, causal resample ablation can isolate and test each direction of information flow. Ablating the chest-to-wrist pathway doubles error, whereas the reverse costs far less. Encoding hemodynamic structure into attention routing thus improves real-world sensing robustness and enables rigorous auditing of multi-sensor fusion.

2611.28354.title: Understanding Membership Inference Attacks on EEG Models
2611.28354.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) signals contain sensitive, subject-specific information, making models trained on them potential targets for membership inference attacks (MIAs). Although MIAs have been studied extensively in other domains, their applications to EEG models are relatively scarce, and the factors driving the vulnerability of EEG models to MIAs are not adequately understood. In this paper, we present a systematic empirical analysis of MIAs on EEG models using three datasets, seven model architectures, four attack methods, and two metrics. Results show that poor model generalization (large train-test loss and accuracy gap) is the strongest indicator of MIA vulnerability. Longer training and larger models also increase vulnerability. Moreover, no particular scalp region, frequency band, inter-channel correlation pattern, or temporal versus spectral representation of EEG data consistently explains MIA vulnerability across datasets. Finally, subject identification and leave-one-subject-out experiments indicate that models relying more heavily on subject-specific representations are more vulnerable to MIAs. Overall, our findings identify the key drivers of membership leakage in EEG models and can provide guidance for developing MIA-resilient EEG systems.

2611.28349.title: Grammar-as-a-Draft: More Tokens per Speculative Decoding Step on Grammar-Constrained Structured Outputs
2611.28349.abstract: Under structured outputs (JSON schemas, regexes, tool calls), speculative drafters do not see the grammar constraint and repeatedly propose invalid keys, delimiters, and indentation, while the grammar engine already knows which tokens must come next. We present Grammar-as-a-Draft (GaaD), which treats the grammar as a second drafter. Before each verify step, the scheduler merges the drafter's proposal with grammar-forced tokens into one draft row: matching tokens stay as GRAMMAR, the proposal is cut where it leaves the forced path, and forced tokens fill the rest of a row wider than the drafter's proposal. The verify step accepts GRAMMAR drafts without computing their logits, composing with any drafter with no new kernels or compilation on the critical path. Because grammars fix text rather than tokens, committing canonical forced tokens changes the output distribution relative to grammar-masked target decoding. We implement GaaD in vllm-torchtpu and an independent Rust serving runtime, evaluating on TPU v7x with MTP, DFlash, and n-gram drafters on a JSON character-profile benchmark. GaaD raises average acceptance length from 2.06 to 5.43 (MTP, Qwen3.5-0.8B), 1.99 to 5.31 (MTP, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B), 1.57 to 4.13 (DFlash, Qwen3-4B), and 1.30 to 3.64 (n-gram, Qwen3-4B), decoding 2.66-2.81x faster at batch size 1 and 1.14-1.70x at batch size 64. In Rust, MTP+GaaD is 2.23x faster on Qwen3.5-0.8B, 2.02x on Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8, and 1.22x at 128 concurrent requests. Under mixed traffic (25-50% structured), GaaD finishes the workload 1.03-1.23x sooner (structured requests 2.2-3.2x sooner) while plain-text TPOT rises 7-42%. We also show grammar-masked greedy decoding can pick non-canonical tokenizations, so GaaD can yield different valid outputs that an fp32 reference finds equally likely.

2611.28298.title: Language Model Harnesses can be Compositional Generalizers
2611.28298.abstract: Modern language models (LMs) are post-trained and deployed as agents inside a "harness", but standard harness designs accumulate context that the neural network is forced to generalize to, making training for long-horizon tasks expensive and time-consuming. We study an alternative emerging path: training inherently neurosymbolic LM harnesses, which externalize and manage context programmatically to compose existing LM capabilities. We hypothesize that training around these harnesses can offer a better return on compute by enabling compositional generalization, as they can learn to decompose complex problems so that every observation their neural LM receives is locally in-distribution, even when the full task is novel. We find that harnesses like the Recursive Language Model (RLM) learn such decompositions readily under reinforcement learning post-training: (1) we demonstrate that training only on short tasks can generalize to tasks 2-64$\times$ longer while the base neural LM improves less, and (2) training on one domain transfers to novel domains that share latent structure. On messier, complex tasks, we find that we can target individual LLM calls within a harness by generating and training on easier, synthetically generated surrogate environments with fake tool / sub-calls, a technique we call surrogate harness training. From this finding, we train RLM-27B on synthetic data, and show it improves Qwen3.8-27B in the same RLM harness on a hard suite of long-context tasks like CTC-Bench and ExpertLongBench by 26.9% on average while using $\sim$2$\times$ fewer tokens at inference time. Finally, we show that harnesses can compose over these newly learned decompositions using recursive sub-harness calls.

2611.28294.title: MRI-Driven Dual-Energy CT Synthesis via Conditional Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models for MRI-only Radiotherapy and Protontherapy
2611.28294.abstract: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides excellent soft-tissue contrast without ionizing radiation but lacks the electron-density information needed for radiotherapy dose calculation. Dual-energy computed tomography (DECT) improves tissue characterization and stopping-power ratio (SPR) estimation for proton therapy, but requires additional radiation exposure. We developed a denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) to synthesize high- and low-energy CT (sHECT and sLECT) simultaneously from a single MRI scan. Retrospective paired MRI-DECT data from patients receiving head-and-neck proton therapy were used to train and evaluate a multi-decoder DDPM with SwinViT or ResUNet denoisers. Performance was compared with Pix2PixGAN and CycleGAN using image-quality metrics, Hounsfield unit (HU) errors, anatomical profiles, and SPR maps and uncertainties. The DDPM outperformed both generative adversarial network baselines in visual fidelity and quantitative image quality. For sHECT and sLECT, respectively, mean absolute errors were 36.29 +/- 5.25 and 43.72 +/- 6.77 HU; peak signal-to-noise ratios were 27.44 +/- 1.06 and 26.26 +/- 0.98 dB; structural similarity indices were 0.89 +/- 0.02 and 0.87 +/- 0.03; and normalized cross-correlations were 0.95 +/- 0.01 and 0.94 +/- 0.01. The synthesized images preserved anatomical boundaries, while uncertainties in derived SPR maps remained within the expected acceptable range. MRI-based DECT synthesis using DDPM may provide tissue-specific information for proton therapy planning while reducing the need for radiation-based DECT acquisition.

2611.28231.title: Evaluating Memanto on DolphinBench for AI Agents
2611.28231.abstract: Memory benchmarks built on question answering tell an agent which fact to recall. Workplace requests often leave that need implicit: to post an update in the team's channel, an agent must work out which channel from earlier interactions and use it in a tool call. We evaluate Memanto, a memory agent that ranks memories with an information-theoretic relevance score, on DolphinBench, which tests memory through 600 simulated workplace tasks, each validated as requiring memory. Running in the Hermes agent harness with GPT-6-Luna and at most 6 iterations per conversation, Memanto completes 503 tasks (83.83%). The strongest configuration reported by the benchmark's authors, Mem0 with GPT-5.6-Luna and up to 60 iterations, completes 424 (70.67%). Memanto's run also has the lowest total cost ($10.86, against $61.48 for the cheapest reported run) and the shortest median task latency (15.32s). Grading uses the benchmark's own judge, but the agent model differs, so these results compare complete systems. The memory system affects both whether an agent completes such tasks and what completion costs.

2611.28194.title: HEP-Ex-Bench: Evaluating Agentic Performance in High Energy Physics Experiment Data Analyses with Sealed Worlds
2611.28194.abstract: Agentic systems are increasingly being explored for automating experimental high-energy physics measurements, but the correctness of their results can today be reliably evaluated only via extensive expert review. To address this, we propose a method to perform detailed quantitative evaluations of agent-driven analyses through the use of blind analysis and injection tests, which are critical in a typical expert review. Agents develop a data analysis pipeline on a public dataset, while the evaluation is performed on programmatically generated sealed private datasets where signals are injected and simulation settings varied within realistic detector uncertainties. By requiring agents to provide a single workflow that is evaluated across these "sealed worlds", we are able to test the accuracy and robustness of the workflows. We demonstrate the approach on four tasks built from CMS open data and present it as a way to reliably benchmark scientific work in experimental high-energy physics. At the time of writing, the best-performing model, Gemini 4 Argon, reaches 60% of the score of the expert reference analyses on average, ahead of GPT 6 Astra at 38% and Claude Opus 5.5 at 31%. In individual sessions on one of the tasks, Gemini 4 Argon exceeds the reference. The benchmark is hosted at https://hep-ex-bench.github.io

2611.28175.title: A world model for longitudinal health-trajectory prediction in older adults across multinational cohorts
2611.28175.abstract: Aging is characterized by continuously evolving health states, yet most existing prediction models focus on static health risk at isolated time points rather than explicitly modelling how health trajectories unfold over time. We developed a health world model based on the Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture to represent evolving health states and simulate future trajectories under specified actions. The model combines a state encoder, an action- and context-conditioned predictor, a stop-gradient target encoder, and clinical outcome heads. We trained the model on the US Health and Retirement Study (HRS) and evaluated it without refitting in the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA) and the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS). Open-loop evaluation assessed discrimination and calibration for mortality and worsening of activities of daily living (ADL) and instrumental activities of daily living (IADL). In the held-out HRS test set, the areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROCs) for mortality, ADL worsening, and IADL worsening were 0.89, 0.93, and 0.93 at the first horizon and 0.84, 0.84, and 0.85 at the fifth horizon, respectively. Predicted risks stratified subsequent outcomes across horizons. Across the evaluated horizons, mortality AUROC ranged from 0.867 to 0.881 in ELSA and from 0.796 to 0.801 in CHARLS. Simulated trajectories preserved the expected risk ordering across predefined action regimes. In counterfactual simulations, changes in lifestyle actions shifted predicted risks in directions consistent with observed associations. The model provides a framework for longitudinal risk prediction and action-conditioned simulation in older adults.

2611.28173.title: Selective Verification in Multi-Agent Orchestration with Large Language Models
2611.28173.abstract: Agents can agree because they relied on the same flawed evidence. We use an exact model of nine binary votes to examine when a verifier should intervene. In the main comparison, workers err 20 percent of the time under ordinary conditions, shared failures occur in 10 percent of cases, and the verifier errs 2 percent of the time in either state. When worker error during a shared failure is 80 percent, checking close votes yields 7.93 percent verdict error, compared with 9.06 percent for random checks at the same expected check rate. The ordering reverses at 90 percent worker error during failure. At the matched check rate for that regime, checking close votes yields 9.98 percent error, random checks yield 9.41 percent, and ranking checks by their expected error reduction yields 6.73 percent. The model also shows that passing branch vote counts preserves the flat majority and reduces the number of messages the root receives. A design guide and a documentation audit of four Python frameworks translate these findings into implementation choices.

2611.28159.title: How Far Can LLMs Go in Generating Android Lint Checks from Natural Language?
2611.28159.abstract: Static analysis tools such as Android Lint, PMD, and CodeQL let developers add custom checks for project-specific rules. However, authoring a check is a demanding programming task: a rule can be stated in a few sentences, yet turning it into a working, tested check requires detailed knowledge of the analysis framework and its issue-detection logic. Recent work generates such checks with large language models (LLMs), but each system needs more than the natural language description a developer always has: a bug-fix patch, a CVE record, or a developer-written test suite to repair against. No prior work measures whether an LLM can turn a description into a working check, or what external knowledge it needs to do so. We introduce LintBench, a human-validated benchmark of 113 real-world Android Lint checks, each paired with a natural language description and its original test suite as a held-out oracle. We evaluate four LLMs, including proprietary and open-weight models. We compare prompting strategies, then evaluate execution-guided repair with and without retrieved API knowledge. Prompting alone reaches 30%-65% (pass@5) across models. Execution-guided repair and retrieval reach 57%-85% test-passing rates within five calls. Our results show that execution feedback raises the pass rate, while retrieved framework knowledge raises the compile rate, which reaches up to 99%. The framework knowledge helps the low-performing models the most, providing the knowledge they need to fix compilation errors. Of the generated checks that compile but fail their tests, 87% have false negatives, missing an issue the generated check should report. Based on our findings, getting the issue-detection logic right remains an open challenge. We release LintBench and the evaluation harness to support future work on generating Android Lint checks.

2611.28158.title: Measuring and Teaching Language Model Agents to Act on Delayed Consequences
2611.28158.abstract: Language model agents are increasingly asked to run ongoing multi-day operations rather than finish isolated single-turn tasks. In daily operations, today's choices reshape later observations and cash constraints because empty shelves hide lost walk-in demand, short-shipped customers quietly shrink future orders weeks later, and emergency buying drains working capital. We introduce SMB Bench, a calibrated 90-day wholesale simulator with 18 causally paired tasks and an 859-run frontier trace dataset, to ask what experience and learning signal make an agent better at noticing, attributing, and acting on the delayed consequences of its own decisions in unseen businesses. Across 16 frontier models, only 3 outperform a fixed buying rule; models often record a relevant diagnosis in their notes without changing later purchases in time, showing that diagnosing a problem, changing behavior, and improving a business are separate achievements. To study how experience improves those failures in an open model (Qwen3.8-27B), we used training-business records to identify operational rules and archived frontier quarters as starting states to continue from rather than transcripts to copy. On an unseen test business under identical evaluation instructions, the trained policy followed customer-protection commitments more consistently and reduced severe-loss quarters, while the additional profit benefit remained uncertain. Carrying those commitments through the quarter exposed the cost of fulfilling them, as early-quarter stocking habits left the buyer relying on emergency supply and a deteriorating supplier. The results separate recognizing a delayed effect, acting on it consistently, and coordinating surrounding decisions so that the response improves profit. SMB Bench connects these observations to a learning method by turning archived decisions and their consequences into reusable training experience.

2611.28153.title: From Observation to Explanation: Mechanistic Interpretability of LLM-Generated Code for Principled Repair
2611.28153.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have transformed software development, yet our understanding of how they generate code remains critically underdeveloped. We address this gap by triangulating evidence across three layers. Longitudinally, autonomous agent-attributed code is statistically indistinguishable from human code under a semantic modification definition (HR = 1.019, p = 0.490), yet attracts disproportionately corrective modifications in production (49.1% vs 37.9% human baseline). This finding demands a causal explanation. Empirically, existing benchmarks overestimate LLM capabilities: models that achieve 84 to 89% correctness on synthetic tasks attain only 24 to 35% on real-world class-level code. Behaviourally, detection systems reveal puzzling asymmetries: GPT-3.5 is far more detectable than modern models (AUC-ROC = 0.96, a 27-point gap), even though modern models produce mutually similar code structures; yet no single feature reliably distinguishes AI-generated from human code at the class level, and the leading commercial detector achieves only 15 to 64% recall. Together, these findings raise a question that empirical studies cannot answer: why do LLMs generate code with these properties? This thesis proposes mechanistic interpretability, a causal token-level circuit tracing, as the bridge between empirical observation and principled correction. By identifying the transformer circuits responsible for detectable stylistic signatures, hallucination patterns, and systematic defects, we aim to drive an agentic repair framework that intervenes at the causal source of defects rather than patching surface symptoms.

2611.28152.title: STEGOGUARD-LM: Evaluating End-to-End Protection Against LLM Covert Channels
2611.28152.abstract: A defense that disrupts hidden messages may still provide little protection if its detector rarely triggers an intervention. We present StegoGuard-LM, a controlled framework for evaluating defenses against covert messages in large language model outputs. We examine token-rank and synonym channels, with Unicode concealment as a structural control, and track messages through detection, intervention, and recovery. Deterministic rewriting prevented full recovery of 103 of 104 synonym-encoded messages when applied unconditionally, but only one when intervention depended on a detector set to limit false alarms. In a four-round replay on a 48-response subset, an attacker selecting from a fixed catalog recovered more bits by switching channels, although paired gains were not statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Randomized rewriting showed no sustained advantage in this pilot. A more sensitive detector improved protection but modified about one-third of clean responses. These findings show how uneven detection can undermine effective rewriting and why protection must be evaluated alongside attacker adaptation and intervention on legitimate text.

2611.28109.title: Green ACO: An Energy-Aware Ant Colony Optimisation for the MAX-SAT Problem with EI/J Scheduling and Thompson Sampling
2611.28109.abstract: NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems demand heavy computation, and this raises real environmental concerns, especially in regions with carbon-intensive power grids. This paper presents Green ACO, an energy-aware Ant Colony Optimisation algorithm for the MAXIMUM SATISFIABILITY (MAX-SAT) problem. At its core is an Expected Improvement per Joule (EI/J) scheduler. At every iteration, it picks the operator that best balances expected quality gain against expected energy cost. Three operators feed the scheduler: WalkSAT, Focused Variable Neighbourhood Search, and Clause-Restart Greedy, ranging from cheap and surgical to aggressive and costly. An offline dual-regime profiling phase calibrates these operators before the search even begins, and, combined with Thompson sampling, this reduces uninformed early operator choices; online call-count warm-up still occurs. A pre-dispatch guard rejects calls when their estimated energy cost, with a safety multiplier, exceeds the remaining budget. Sparse pheromone updates, pheromone caching across budgets, and stagnation-based early stopping trim energy use further, without hurting solution quality. The framework also incorporates a budget predictor that estimates the energy budget required for unseen instances. On four hard MAX-SAT reference instances, Green ACO reaches an average quality of 98.44%. This beats the standard ACO baselines by close to 3 points, while using only 986 J against 4,171 to 6,610 J for the strongest competitors, a six-and-a-half-fold gain in quality per joule. Under the Algerian grid's carbon intensity, this cuts CO$_2$e emissions by approximately 85% compared with the most energy-hungry baseline.

2611.28103.title: ABCoord: An Artificial Bee Colony (ABC)-Based Decentralized Distributed Two-Layer Decision-Making Architecture for the Coordination of AI Agents
2611.28103.abstract: Rapid progress in large language models (LLMs) is turning AI agents into multi-agent systems that jointly solve complex tasks, and the architecture that coordinates the agents toward a common goal is gaining fundamental importance in these systems. Since centralized architectures can become bottlenecks as the number of agents grows, whereas distributed architectures incur increasing communication costs, a decentralized coordination architecture that scales with low communication cost is needed. Recently, the structure of the artificial bee colony (ABC) algorithm has been defined for the first time as a two-layer decentralized information-processing and decision-making architecture. ABCoord is built on this proposed architecture. The results show that ABCoord, used for the coordination of AI agents, performs at a level comparable to existing architectures on the BigCodeBench benchmark in the self-test condition, in which the tests are also written by the language model. In the oracle condition, in which the solutions are evaluated with the official tests, the number of solved problems increases considerably.

2611.28082.title: Frontier Open-Weight AI Risk Management Framework
2611.28082.abstract: Open-weight models advance transparency, research, and innovation, and spread the benefits of AI more widely. They also carry distinct risks. A release cannot be undone, safeguards can be removed through fine-tuning, and no single party can monitor use or withdraw the model. Managing these risks therefore requires an approach tailored to open release. This framework addresses the governance challenge at the heart of that choice. Co-developed by Concordia AI and Z.AI, it adapts the full risk management lifecycle, from risk assessment to mitigation and governance, to the unique properties of open-weight models. This document does not resolve every tension between openness and safety. Rather, it provides the first comprehensive, evidence-based foundation for navigating these tensions. As frontier open-weight releases accelerate, risk management best practice and standards are urgently needed. We invite researchers, developers, policymakers, and civil society to build on this framework and advance the science and practice of open-weight AI governance.

2611.28055.title: SnakeTranslate: Weakly Supervised Policy Learning from Offline Parallel Text for Simultaneous Translation
2611.28055.abstract: Adaptive simultaneous translation requires reliable prefix translation and timely READ/WRITE decisions, but ordinary parallel corpora provide no action annotations. We present SnakeTranslate, which adapts loss-derived alignment to sampled causal histories for jointly learning both capabilities. The framework supports supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on parallel text and on-policy distillation (OPD) with reverse Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence on student-generated translations. At inference, source and target tokens form one append-only interleaved history, enabling incremental decoding with cache reuse. On FLEURS, NTREX128, and WMT24++, our 4B model improves quality--latency trade-offs over streaming policies applied to the same offline-tuned backbone, with further gains from OPD. It also compares favorably with larger translation models at low and moderate latency, while higher-latency quality gaps remain on WMT24++.

2611.28050.title: Benchmarking and Adapting LLMs for English-Swedish Medical Question Answering
2611.28050.abstract: Large language models do well on English medical exams, but less is known about Swedish. This matters most for small open models that hospitals can run locally. To reduce this gap, we first build an item-aligned English-Swedish benchmark from ten medical multiple-choice datasets; each Swedish item keeps the options and answer of its English source. A conservative refinement loop repairs the translations: open models from three families find errors, ground them in a Swedish medical term base, and keep a model-written edit only if blind judges vote for it. On this benchmark, small models lose much more accuracy in Swedish than large ones, especially when they answer without reasoning. Second, we ask whether English data and open teacher models can close this gap. We translate the training data, let teachers write reasoning traces, and fine-tune two small students on gold answers or traces in English, Swedish, or both. Training on reasoning traces that include Swedish closes the gap and lifts the 1.2B student from 23.5\% to 52.0\% in Swedish, slightly above a 20B open model in its fast mode, with a sixth of its memory. We release the benchmark, its edit history, and the code.

2611.28048.title: Distributionally-Verifiable Rewards for Human-Behavior Simulation
2611.28048.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate survey respondents in social-science research. A useful simulator should predict individual responses, reproduce population response distributions, and capture demographic differences. Common training approaches struggle to balance these goals: exact-match rewards encourage the model to concentrate on the most frequent human response, which is contradictory to the goal of distributional alignment. Meanwhile, aggregate distribution matching can look good even when demographic information is ignored. To this end, we introduce Distributionally-Verifiable Rewards (DVR), a reinforcement-learning reward that uses demographic group distribution gaps to guide individual responses, designed by aligning policy generated frequencies with human response frequencies within each question-group margins. We evaluate the method using the OpinionQA dataset and find that comparing with accuracy-only RLVR, DVR preserves per-response accuracy while reducing JSD by 34.5% in-distribution and 14.6% on held-out questions, with higher DPC point estimates on both splits. Comparing KL-SFT with the demographics-blind marginal further shows that low JSD is insufficient to establish fidelity to population heterogeneity, highlighting that accuracy, distributional fit, and demographic structure should be evaluated together.

2611.12603.title: Direct Conditioning of Audio Diffusion Transformers on fMRI Reveals Cortical Contributions to Sound Reconstruction
2611.12603.abstract: Reconstructing audio from brain activity remains challenging. Existing brain-to-audio pipelines typically map neural responses to predefined stimulus representations before synthesis. While recent work in the visual domain has explored direct conditioning on brain activity, this approach has not yet been extended to audio diffusion models. We introduce MAAS (Multi-Area Auditory Synthesis), an end-to-end framework that conditions a pretrained audio diffusion transformer on ROI-wise fMRI responses without first supervising a decoder to predict an external stimulus representation. MAAS uses region-specific projections and learned brain tokens to condition Stable Audio through a dedicated cross-attention pathway. On a 7T fMRI dataset, we demonstrate consistent improvements over baselines, including two-stage fMRI-to-latent conditioning, across both acoustic and semantic evaluation metrics. In addition, we introduce a fidelity metric grounded in a computational model of auditory neural processing, which allows us to quantify the contribution of individual auditory cortical regions to reconstructed audio representations.

2611.29861.title: Where does pancreatic lesion segmentation fail on public CT? An attenuation-stratified analysis of a duct-guided pipeline on PanTS
2611.29861.abstract: Lesion segmentation is a building block of most CT pipelines for pancreatic cancer detection, yet lesion overlap scores stay low. Instead of proposing a new architecture, we report where an end-to-end pipeline fails on a large public dataset. On PanTS we built a three-stage pipeline: pancreas segmentation, maps of the main pancreatic duct (MPD) and common bile duct (CBD), and a lesion model that receives the CT with or without the predicted duct maps. Both lesion models were trained identically on 4007 scans and evaluated once on 737 held-out test scans (127 with a lesion) under a comparison rule fixed before the test run. Lesion Dice was 0.213 with duct maps and 0.209 with CT only (paired difference +0.004, 95% CI -0.011 to +0.019). The duct maps raised the share of lesions touched by a prediction (+0.079, 95% CI +0.024 to +0.134) but also enlarged predictions in lesion-free scans, and lesion-like regions were predicted in all lesion-free test scans. Out of fold, keeping only the predicted components that touched the lesion raised Dice only from 0.285 to 0.309; the loss came mainly from the extent of correctly located predictions. Clearly hypoattenuating lesions, which intensity alone separates from normal pancreas, had the lowest coverage (median 16.6%). From the predicted maps alone, the MPD diameter separated lesion from lesion-free test scans with AUC 0.794 (95% CI 0.747 to 0.839), while the CBD diameter was weak (AUC 0.603) and added nothing. Code for training, inference and evaluation is publicly available.

2611.28934.title: Neural Grey: Practical Vignetting Calibration from Casual Camera Rolls
2611.28934.abstract: Neural Grey estimates a reusable camera-lens shading map from four approximate roll captures of a static, light-colored surface. Rolling the camera moves wall illumination across the sensor while lens shading stays fixed. We fit these two fields jointly, together with small pose and exposure errors, using a physical shading envelope and compact bounded neural residuals. Rotation alone, however, cannot distinguish radial lens attenuation from radial wall illumination. A focal-conditioned radial selector addresses this ambiguity: it uses focal length and sensor size to choose the broad radial profile while retaining the fitted spatial remainder. Component and sensitivity studies separate the roles of the field representation, radial selection, and numerical settings. Neural Grey reaches 25.43 dB on 100 synthetic cases, 24.49 dB on ray-traced lens architectures, and 25.38 dB on 21 real takes from seven optical configurations. On the real benchmark, it exceeds the strongest competing mean by 5.62 dB and wins five of seven configurations.

2611.28740.title: US-Seg: One Reference for Universal Ultrasound Segmentation
2611.28740.abstract: Recent ultrasound foundation models have demonstrated strong feature extraction capabilities across organs, tasks, and imaging conditions. However, converting these representations into segmentation still requires finetuning on annotated target data. To reduce reliance on task-specific finetuning, existing universal ultrasound segmentation methods typically adopt prompt-based target specification, mainly through spatial prompts in SAM-style models or task prompts exemplified by MOFO. Yet, directly segmenting targets unseen during training still requires repeated per-image interaction or target-specific adaptation. We propose US-Seg, a universal ultrasound segmentation framework that uses only a single annotated reference to specify the target and directly predicts its mask in query images without finetuning. The fundamental insight of US-Seg is to reformulate segmentation from direct image-to-label mapping for predefined targets into a shared structural recovery process learned from heterogeneous reference-query pairs through masked label reconstruction, thereby making a single reference sufficient for target specification. Boundary-centric label masking emphasizes ambiguous boundaries, encouraging transferable structural cues rather than target-specific appearance patterns. Using these structure-enriched representations, multi-level bidirectional reference-query interaction aligns the reference-defined target with the query. Finally, a prediction-aware iterative decoder uses intermediate predictions to progressively correct residual structural errors under reference guidance. Without repeated interaction or laborious annotation, US-Seg achieves an average Dice of 81.85% across six evaluations covering cross-site and cross-task generalization, outperforming the strongest label-reference method by 24.30%, while also delivering the best in-domain performance.

2611.30032.title: Model-Assisted Probability of Detection Studies for Image-Based Human Inspection
2611.30032.abstract: Establishing a probability of detection (POD) curve is important for assessing the reliability of components in aging systems. Traditional POD studies rely on physical specimens containing representative flaws and human inspectors who record detection results, making such studies costly. This paper demonstrates how appropriately validated physics-based simulation can substantially reduce, and in suitable applications potentially replace, physical POD experiments. We use XRSIM, an X-ray radiographic simulator, to generate weld images containing cracks of varying size, morphology, and location. Flaw characteristics, locations, and the number of flaws per image were randomized, with images containing zero to three flaws. Each simulated flaw is treated as an observational unit contributing flaw-level hit-miss responses. To capture human inspection variability, the images were presented in random order to five inspectors, each of whom inspected the images twice. The resulting data were analyzed using a repeated-measures binary-regression model accounting for flaw-to-flaw, inspector-to-inspector, flaw/inspector-combination, and inspection-to-inspection variability. Bayesian inference was used to estimate the population-mean POD curve, inspector-specific POD curves, and associated statistical uncertainty. Results show that flaw-to-flaw variability dominates, with appreciable differences among inspectors. The study provides a framework for combining physics-based image simulation with controlled human inspection to estimate POD while reducing the experimental burden of physical specimen fabrication.

2611.29177.title: Rateless Lattice Codes over Fading Wiretap Channels: Finite-Length Secrecy and the Secret-Key Capacity of Degraded Sessions
2611.29177.abstract: In rateless transmission the transmitter keeps sending until the legitimate receiver (Bob) can decode. Over a wiretap channel this has a useful side effect: the eavesdropper (Eve) sees only as many symbols as Bob needs, although the transmitter knows neither channel. We study the secrecy of rateless lattice codes in this setting. First, using a public dither and privacy amplification, we prove a finite-length secrecy bound, in total variation distance, for every channel realization, even if Eve knows all codes and seeds and combines all packets. Second, stopping when Bob acknowledges successful decoding, as in hybrid ARQ, costs at most the logarithm of the number of possible feedback outcomes in secret bits. Third, for degraded sessions with state-based stopping and without a pre-shared key or other public discussion, the secret-key rate of a session cannot exceed its accumulated Gaussian secrecy capacity, and adaptive key generation with shaped rateless lattice codes comes within any $\epsilon>0$ of this limit when Eve's channel states are revealed after the session. If only their statistics are known, choosing the key length after the session guarantees a prescribed secrecy-outage probability. Finally, over block Rayleigh fading with a CRC-based acknowledgement and joint belief-propagation decoding, and with Eve $20$~dB weaker on average, the scheme reaches $59$--$69\%$ of the outage-weighted throughput of an ideal infinite-length secure hybrid-ARQ benchmark for Bob SNRs of $8$--$20$~dB.
